opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to just start doing the work, even before anyone's paying you to do it. A lot of people wait until they feel "qualified," and in my experience that feeling rarely arrives on its own. It comes from having built things.

On the engineering side, which is where I spend most of my time, the skills that matter most are often less glamorous than people expect. Being able to write clean, fast code, debug a large distributed system, figure out why a training run is behaving strangely, and dig through a messy codebase someone else wrote. You can practice all of that on your own. Pick a paper you find interesting, try to reimplement it, and when your results don't match, figure out why. That debugging process teaches you a huge amount, and it's very close to what the day-to-day work actually looks like.

I'd also say don't underestimate strong software engineering experience from outside of ML. Some of the people who've had the biggest impact on our team came from backgrounds like infrastructure or systems work rather than research. The research ideas matter, but a lot of progress comes from making things run reliably at scale, and people with that experience can pick up the ML-specific parts surprisingly quickly.

The other piece is to engage seriously with the safety questions themselves. Read the work that's out there, form your own views, and notice where you disagree. We care a lot that people understand why the work matters and can think independently about the risks, not just that they're technically strong.

And finally, just apply. People screen themselves out far too often. The worst case is you get a no and learn something about what to work on next. Lots of people I work with didn't feel ready when they applied.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting the work before being hired and gives examples of practicing relevant engineering tasks independently.

r002.rationale: It says doing the work builds skills, but does not say this helps determine whether someone wants the role.

r003.rationale: It does not compare demonstrated work performance with performance on interview questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that people are often much more qualified than they think they are. We get a lot of applicants who've kind of talked themselves out of applying because they assume they need to have a PhD or have published a bunch of papers or whatever, and that's really not the bar. Most of the people on my team didn't come in with a deep machine learning background. I didn't, really. So I'd encourage people to just apply, honestly, even if they don't feel ready.

But if you do want to prepare, I think the most important thing by far is just being a really strong engineer. A lot of the work of training large models is actually engineering work. It's distributed systems, it's debugging things at scale, it's writing code that runs on thousands of chips without falling over. And so if you're a good software engineer who's comfortable with Python and can reason carefully about performance and can debug hard problems, you're most of the way there. The ML-specific knowledge you can pick up relatively quickly once you're in the environment.

Beyond that, I'd say do some kind of project. Not a huge one, but something where you actually train a model yourself, end to end. Implement a transformer from scratch, train it on some dataset, try to make it go faster, try to figure out why your loss curve looks weird. That kind of hands-on experience teaches you way more than reading papers, and it also gives you something concrete to talk about in an interview. We care a lot about whether someone can take a vague problem and make progress on it, and a project is a good way to demonstrate that.

And then the last thing I'd say is, the interview process is going to be pretty close to the actual work. So if you practice coding problems that look like real engineering tasks, not just leetcode puzzles but things like "here's a system, make it faster" or "here's a bug, find it," that's good preparation. And if you go through the process and don't get an offer, that's genuinely fine. People reapply all the time, and a lot of them get in on the second or third try after another year of building skills. So I wouldn't treat it as a one-shot thing.

r001.rationale: The response recommends an independent, hands-on project: training a model end to end, improving it, and debugging it, which mirrors work involved in the role.

r002.rationale: The project is described as a way to learn and demonstrate skills, but the response does not say it helps determine whether someone wants the role.

r003.rationale: The response says realistic engineering tasks are good interview preparation and that a project demonstrates ability, but does not compare work performance as evidence against performance on interview questions.

astra-6.text:
I think the best preparation is usually to find something where you can do real work and get feedback quickly. If you want to be a research engineer, for example, pick a project that involves implementing a paper, training a model, or figuring out why an experiment isn’t working. Try to get to the point where you can make progress independently, rather than just following a tutorial.

And I wouldn’t make the goal too narrowly “become qualified for Anthropic.” Look for opportunities to work with people you can learn a lot from and build skills that would be useful across a range of roles. That might be another job, a research collaboration, or a project you pursue yourself.

I’d also distinguish between not feeling qualified and actually lacking the skills. You don’t need to resolve all your uncertainty before applying. Let the application process give you some information, while continuing to do work that helps you improve.

r001.rationale: Recommends doing real work on a self-pursued project, such as implementing a paper or training a model, to prepare for the role.

r002.rationale: Does not say that doing the work helps determine whether someone wants the role.

r003.rationale: Does not compare demonstrated role performance with interview-question performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d encourage people not to make the goal too narrowly “get a job at Anthropic.” Think about the kind of work you’d want to do, and find opportunities to get better at it. If that’s research or engineering, doing a project where you have to solve a real problem can be a good way to learn and to demonstrate what you can do.

And I wouldn’t necessarily wait until you feel fully qualified before applying. You can let the hiring process give you some information about that. In parallel, keep pursuing work that builds useful skills and that you’d be excited about even if it didn’t lead to a particular role.

r001.rationale: It recommends doing a project that solves a real problem, but does not clearly state that the work should be done independently outside Anthropic.

r002.rationale: It suggests thinking about what kind of work you want, but does not say that doing that work helps determine whether you want the role.

r003.rationale: It says a project can demonstrate ability and that applying can provide information, but does not compare work performance with interview performance.
